passages.original: ipsa vero Χάρυβδις a qua imago ducitur, maritima est. Pessime igitur dicitur ποντοχάρυβδις. Immo fuit addendum aliquid quo vel ubi habitet altera illa Charybdis significetur (ut γαστροχάρυβδις quidam audit apud Cratinum Ι 121 Kock) vel quid devoret. Alterum praetuli; cf. Ps.-Plautinum parasitum cui nomen fuit Πολτοφαγωνίδης (cf. Ritschl op. IIl p. 328). Wachsmuthius. V. 2. Hesychius: ἐγγαστριμάχαιραν· τὴν ἐν τῇ γαστρὶ κατατέμνουσαν.
passages.english: But Charybdis herself, from whom the image is drawn, belongs to the sea. So *pontocharybdis* ("sea-Charybdis") is a very bad expression. Rather, something should have been added to indicate either where that other Charybdis lives (as a certain man is called *gastrocharybdis* ["belly-Charybdis"] in Cratinus, I 121 Kock) or what she devours. I have preferred the latter; compare the parasite in Pseudo-Plautus whose name was *Poltophagōnidēs* ("Porridge-eater") (cf. Ritschl, Opuscula III p. 328). Wachsmuth. Line 2. Hesychius: *engastrimachaira*: "the one that cuts up inside the belly."
passages.notes: The passage is a Latin commentary note on a Greek fragment; the conjecture discussed (from the preceding context) is *poltocharybdis* ("porridge-Charybdis") for transmitted *pontocharybdis*. "IIl" in the Ritschl reference is read as III (scanning error). "Op." is taken as Ritschl's Opuscula.
